name: Existing products and precedents: Monotype/MyFonts AI Search, Adobe Fonts tags and the Adobe Express intent model, FontBase SuperSearch, Fonts In Use, Typewolf, Fontjoy, IDEO Font Map, tfrere/fontmap, TypeSeek
what_it_is: Nine comparators, each reduced to what it teaches. (1) Monotype / MyFonts AI Search: type a mood, brand trait or use ('warm, modern, a little playful'; 'grounded and trustworthy for a financial brand'), get inventory-aware recommendations with a 'Why this font?' explanation and chat follow-ups ('show only serif'), over 250,000+ fonts from 4,500+ foundry partners. MyFonts US launch November 2025, UK 9 February 2026, press announcement 26 February 2026, MyFonts app in ChatGPT 27 May 2026. Internals undisclosed; the support page says prompts may be processed by third-party systems including enterprise ChatGPT. (2) Adobe Fonts: 26 curated tags plus classification and properties (weight, width, x-height, caps, numbers) as filters; and the Adobe Express intent model (Sharma, Kumar, Zheng, King, SIGIR eCom 2023): text goes to an intent model (1,500+ intents mined from designer-written template tags, DistilBERT), intents go to font vectors where each font is represented by its top 7 intents, trained on about 470,000 text-font-intent triplets from about 212,000 template texts, 2,043 font families. (3) FontBase SuperSearch: four properties measured from each font file when it is added (x-height, weight as black-area ratio, contrast, proportion), combinable as presets or numbers; paid ('Awesome') feature. Slant is not mentioned. (4) Fonts In Use: an archive of real typography in use (about 34,700 entries) tagged by topics, formats, typefaces, contributors and years; topics include Sports (862 uses), Transportation (358), Automotive (334). (5) Typewolf: one curator's lists by class, use and mood (brutalist, hipster, 1970s album covers, quirky grotesques) and a popularity ranking. (6) Fontjoy (Jack Qiao, July 2018): font pairing from CNN embeddings of about 1,861 Google fonts (TensorFlow, open source) with a contrast slider. (7) IDEO Font Map (Kevin Ho, 2017): VGG16 features of about 800 Google fonts reduced with t-SNE to a 2D map; fontmap.ideo.com no longer resolves. (8) tfrere/fontmap (created 2026-08-06, last push 2026-09-30, MIT, 22 stars): FontCLIP embeddings plus t-SNE of Google Fonts, predicted Google sub-styles by logistic regression, scored against Google's tags; no text search. (9) TypeSeek (GitHub Ojochogwu866/use-typeseek, created 2026-09-17, last push 2026-09-20, 0 stars, no licence): SigLIP embeddings and pgvector over Google Fonts, per-font tags written from a rendered image through the Anthropic API with a local SigLIP fallback, evaluated by hit@1/5/10 and MRR against designer-curated lists.
provider_and_url: Monotype AI Search: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/monotype-launches-ai-search-transforming-font-search-and-discovery-with-natural-language-and-conversational-ai-302698367.html , https://support.monotype.com/en/articles/12541008-ai-search , https://www.myfonts.com/blogs/technology-innovation/myfonts-ai-powered-search/ , https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-launches-myfonts-app-chatgpt-bringing-real-font-discovery-ai . Adobe Fonts tags: https://blog.adobe.com/en/publish/2020/08/14/using-tags-to-find-the-perfect-font-for-the-job ; Adobe Express intent model: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08188 . FontBase: https://fontba.se/blog/super-search , https://forum.fontba.se/t/visible-attributes-as-used-by-super-search-and-find-similar/1808 . Fonts In Use: https://fontsinuse.com/ . Typewolf: https://www.typewolf.com/ . Fontjoy: https://experiments.withgoogle.com/fontjoy , https://github.com/Jack000/fontjoy . IDEO Font Map: https://www.designboom.com/design/ideo-font-map-interview-typography-04-21-2017/ . tfrere/fontmap: https://github.com/tfrere/fontmap . TypeSeek: https://github.com/Ojochogwu866/use-typeseek (the earlier name github.com/Ojochogwu866/typeseek now returns 404).
catalog_coverage: None of the nine publishes labels for our 2,099 families, with one partial exception. tfrere/fontmap ships per-font rendering files for 1,877 Google families and variants (README: 1,465 fonts after folding variants; the repo title says 1,100+; a search snippet said 1,192, so the exact figure is [uncertain]). Measured by me from the GitHub tree API for tfrere/fontmap against my re-merged catalog (scratchpad fm_tree.json and merged_catalog_other.json): 1,561 of our 1,760 Google rows match a file by name slug (88.7%, approximate); Fontshare 0 of 64, Velvetyne 0 of 63, Collletttivo 0 of 26, Tunera 0 of 23, Use & Modify 0 of 163. Its pipeline's output is coordinates and predicted sub-styles, not mood labels. Monotype, MyFonts and Adobe Fonts libraries are commercial catalogues, not ours, and expose no data. Fonts In Use and Typewolf cover real-world use and a curator's picks, not a catalogue; counts per family exist only for popular typefaces. FontBase measures whatever fonts the user adds, so in principle all 2,099 (we already read every font with fontkit in src/facts/).
granularity: Monotype and Adobe Fonts: per family (Adobe Express groups similar-looking styles of a family together: 2,043 families). FontBase: per font file (each style measured). fontmap, Fontjoy, IDEO: one rendering per family. Fonts In Use: per real use, with the typeface named. None offers italic or variable-axis positions as a search handle.
signal_type: Mixed. Monotype: semantic, inputs undisclosed. Adobe tags: curated semantic words (26); Adobe Express: learned text-to-font mapping from real usage. FontBase: geometric (measured from files). fontmap, Fontjoy, IDEO, TypeSeek: overall visual look as embeddings (TypeSeek adds written tags). Fonts In Use and Typewolf: human curation of use and mood.
mood_dimensions_covered: MOTION / ACTIVE: none of the nine exposes a motion control. Adobe Fonts' 26 tags (Calligraphy, Clean, Brush Pen, Geometric, Friendly, Rough, Rounded, Cursive, Art Deco, Luxury, Funky, Fun, Futuristic, Marker, Comic, Western, Blackletter, Wedding, School, College, Typewriter, Shaded, Stencil, Inline, Horror, Ornaments; list from a search-result summary of the Adobe tag browser, and its count matches the paper's '26 tags') contain no speed, action or energy word; the nearest are Fun, Funky and Futuristic [uncertain on the exact list]. FontBase measures x-height, weight, contrast and proportion but not slant (not mentioned in the blog). Monotype's free text can express motion, and no test of it is published. Fonts In Use has Sports, Transportation and Automotive topics, which show how designers used type, not how a letter looks; I read the topic names only. Typewolf's navigation shows classification, alternatives, favourites and fun lists (brutalist, hipster, 1970s) and no motion list. OTHER MOODS: Monotype's marketing prompts are multi-trait moods (warm, modern, playful; trustworthy, contemporary, global; refined). Adobe's tags cover Friendly, Fun, Funky, Futuristic, Luxury, Clean. Adobe Express intents are topics and occasions (spooky, wedding, informational, food, 'fast food' as a food topic) and emotional words (happy, encouraging). fontmap and Fontjoy cover look only (no mood words). Net: precedents handle topics, genres and loose multi-trait moods; none shows a tested answer to a tight motion request.
query_style_specificity: The evidence points to loose, multi-word requests. Monotype's own examples are loose ('warm, modern, a little playful'), Adobe Express is evaluated on topic and occasion text, and Adobe's 26-tag system covers only 26 words. Measured-property tools (FontBase) serve tight shape requests (condensed, high contrast, heavy) but say nothing about moods. No precedent publishes results for tight mood words such as 'fast'.
quality_evidence: ADOBE EXPRESS (SIGIR eCom 2023): 75 external evaluators rated 5 recommended fonts for each of 78 high-frequency templates with one text removed: 464 'very good', 216 'ok', 159 'not good', i.e. 81% relevant (680 of 839, computed by me); random fonts and common fonts, as baselines, were each more than 10 percentage points worse; 16 internal annotators on 100 texts gave a mean of 3.67 of 5; in production the click-through rate is above 25% and above 50% of users who click a recommendation export. This rates text-font fit, not mood or motion. TFRERE/FONTMAP: after logistic regression on FontCLIP embeddings, the share of a font's 8 nearest neighbours that share its Google sub-style rose from about 0.31 to about 0.44 on held-out families (README). Its script evaluate_with_gf_tags.py scores embeddings with precision@k against chance, a within-group variant and a linear probe with 5-fold cross-validation, on Google's structural tags only (Sans, Serif, Slab, Script, Monospace, plus Blackletter and Pixel); it does not score the Expressive mood tags. This is a direct template for our held-out test. TYPESEEK: evaluation script reports hit@1/5/10 and MRR against designer-curated acceptance lists and the README admits the numbers 'read low' because the lists are incomplete; no numbers published, and the README was read through a summariser [uncertain]. MONOTYPE / MYFONTS: no published evaluation; vendor claims and one artist quote only; I did not run the live JavaScript search, so nothing is tested by me. FONTBASE, FONTJOY, IDEO, TYPEWOLF, FONTS IN USE: no evaluation published. Net: no precedent has evidence that it answers 'fast movement or action' better than a plain model. The closest relevant evidence is Adobe Express (text to intent to font, 81% relevant) and fontmap's held-out Google-tag test.
known_noise: Adobe Express: 159 of 839 ratings (19%) were 'not good'; intents come from template designers' tags, which are uneven; popular fonts skew results, which the authors countered by describing each font with its top 7 intents. Their raters judged fit to text, a subjective call. fontmap: about 30 Display fonts were corrected by hand after visual review; Playwrite Guides variants were folded into one point. TypeSeek: tags are Claude-written when the API is available and zero-shot SigLIP otherwise, so quality varies by font; the evaluation lists are incomplete. Monotype: unknown; third-party processing; chat history is not kept after a refresh. Fontjoy and IDEO: embeddings group by look and ignore meaning.
name_and_memory_bias: Adobe Express learned from real template usage, so it inherits popularity bias (their common-fonts baseline was more than 10 points worse, showing the bias is real but beatable). Monotype's search runs on a licensed catalogue and shows explanations; whether names influence it is not disclosed. Visual systems (fontmap, TypeSeek, Fontjoy) are name-blind if the render hides the name; TypeSeek's tags come from a model that sees an image. For us, Haiku's memory of popular Google fonts is the same effect, and the prompt already penalises 'very common' fonts.
untagged_rows: Systems built on measured or visual signals (FontBase, fontmap, Fontjoy, TypeSeek) treat every font alike. Systems built on curation or usage leave a silent tail: Adobe Express recommends only from the 2,043 families that appear in templates, so fonts never used in a template are never suggested; Adobe's 26 tags cover an undisclosed subset; Typewolf and Fonts In Use show what one person or the trade chose to show.
text_interference_risk: For the visual precedents: fontmap and TypeSeek render glyph, pangram and weight-strip specimens (README), and CLIP-family models can be swayed by the words rendered, not measured here [uncertain]. FontBase measures shapes without rendering words. The advice from the vision-labels item (neutral specimen text, never the font name) applies if we copy these.
integration_path: Patterns to copy, mapped to server/vibe.ts. (1) Adobe Express pattern, text to intents to fonts: store, per font, a short ranked list of 5 to 7 intent words in a precomputed file server/data/intents.json, format { "<family lower-case>": ["dynamic", "sporty", "techno", ...] }, and add it as one more column in compactCatalog (line 358) only for weakly tagged rows (567 rows with fewer than 3 tags: 513 Google, 53 Use & Modify, 1 Fontshare, measured by me), or for all rows. (2) fontmap pattern, held-out Google tags: copy the scoring idea of evaluate_with_gf_tags.py into server/check-vibe.ts (hide tags, recover them, precision@k against chance). (3) TypeSeek pattern, a model writes tags once per font from a rendered image: this is the vision-labels item; output goes into the same intents.json. (4) FontBase pattern, measured numbers: add slant, contrast and proportion from fontkit (src/facts/) as bucketed words ('slanted', 'condensed', 'high-contrast') in the tags column; this is the measured-traits item. (5) Monotype pattern, explanation: the prompt already asks for a 'reason' per pick under 14 words; ground it in a quoted tag or measured value so it is explainable. Not worth copying: Fontjoy and IDEO (pairing and a map, no text query), Typewolf and Fonts In Use as data (curation, not machine-readable; Fonts In Use blocks automated search).
tokens_per_row: Pattern (1) adds about 8 to 12 tokens per row it touches: about 5,700 tokens for the 567 weakly tagged rows, about 21,000 if all 2,099 rows get it, on top of the current catalog of about 45,000 tokens (characters divided by 3.6, my estimate). Patterns (2), (3) and (4) either add no prompt tokens (offline) or a word or two per row. Everything is static, so the prompt cache keeps working.
vocabulary_alignment: Adobe's 26 tags and Monotype's free-text moods are separate vocabularies from Google's; Adobe Express' 1,500+ intents are topic and occasion words; TypeSeek writes free-text tags; fontmap uses Google's own tags (aligned, but only the structural ones). Adopting any of them adds a vocabulary. The cheapest aligned choice is to aim all new labels at Google's Expressive and Theme words (Active, Excited, Loud, Futuristic, Techno, Calm...) plus a few shape words, as in the impression-datasets item.
explainability: Monotype shows 'Why this font?' text (a model's rationale, not a measurement). FontBase shows measured values. fontmap shows nearest neighbours. Adobe Express shows no reason. Ours can quote a tag or a measured value if the reason line is grounded.
determinism: Embedding and measurement systems (FontBase, fontmap, Fontjoy, IDEO, TypeSeek's vector step) are deterministic. Chat systems (Monotype's, ours) are not, because the model answers differently across runs.
build_effort: Reading these costs nothing more. Building the patterns for an agent in this repo: an intents file written by a model in one batch and checked, about 0.5 day; a held-out Google-tag harness in check-vibe.ts, about 0.5 to 1 day; measured slant, contrast and proportion columns, about 0.5 day (fontkit already loaded); vision tags, 1 to 2 days (other item). The conversational layer Monotype advertises (follow-ups, '#3' references) already exists in the app's prompt.
per_search_cost_and_latency: Monotype's search is free to its users; latency is not published. Adobe Express serves from an Elasticsearch index with precomputed vectors, no figures given. For us, precomputed columns add nothing per search; the existing Haiku call over a cached catalog of about 45,000 tokens is the baseline (I did not measure its latency or run any real search).
one_off_cost: Nothing to borrow patterns. Offline label batches (intents or vision tags for up to 2,099 fonts) use subscription time and belong to the other items.
human_effort: A person rating result grids for 20 to 30 requests: about 1 to 2 hours per round. Adobe used 75 external and 16 internal raters, which is out of reach; one person with the three-level scale (very good, ok, not good) is enough to see a difference of about 10 points. Reviewing an intents file: about 1 to 2 hours for the weak rows.
asset_access: Monotype / MyFonts AI Search: a live JavaScript chat with no public API that I found, and prompts go to third parties; not to be automated. Adobe Fonts: robots.txt blocks only /login and EULA pages (no AI rules), but tag browsing is a JavaScript app and no tag API is documented. FontBase: a desktop app, local. Fonts In Use: robots.txt disallows GPTBot, gives other agents Crawl-delay 10 and Disallow /search (ClaudeBot: delay 1, Disallow /search): do not mine it; read topic pages by hand if needed. Typewolf: read by hand. tfrere/fontmap: MIT repo, data under public/data (1.05 MB font-sprite.svg, 1,877 sentence SVGs); public GitHub API gave me the file list. Fontjoy: open source (Jack000/fontjoy). IDEO Font Map: the domain no longer resolves (DNS lookup failed on 2026-10-03). TypeSeek: public repo, no licence file.
licence_and_provenance: Monotype, Adobe: proprietary, nothing reusable. Fonts In Use content belongs to its contributors. tfrere/fontmap: MIT code; the FontCLIP weights it uses carry their own licence, not checked [uncertain]. Fontjoy: open source on GitHub, licence not checked [uncertain]. TypeSeek: the GitHub API shows license null, which means all rights reserved; do not copy its code. For derived images of our fonts: Google, Velvetyne, Collletttivo, Tunera and Use & Modify fonts are OFL or similar; Fontshare's ITF Free Font License allows use but not redistribution of the font files, so images for a private index are probably fine and published ones need a check.
etiquette: Never velvetyne.fr. Fonts In Use: no automated fetching beyond robots.txt. Monotype: no automation. GitHub: a handful of public API calls (repo metadata and one tree listing), no file downloads.
maintenance_and_freshness: Monotype AI Search is new and expanding (languages, a ChatGPT app in May 2026). The Adobe Express paper is from 2023. Fontjoy (2018) and IDEO's map (2017, domain gone) are dormant. tfrere/fontmap and TypeSeek are weeks old and active (last pushes 2026-09-30 and 2026-09-20), so expect them to change or vanish; the TypeSeek repo appears to have been renamed already (the old URL returns 404). FontBase SuperSearch date unknown [uncertain].
risks_and_limitations: Marketing is not evidence: Monotype's claims are the vendor's, with no comparison on tight mood or motion requests. Most precedents solve other problems (pairing, similarity, identification), and the three that map text to fonts (Monotype, Adobe Express, TypeSeek) either hide internals, were tested on text-font fit, or publish no numbers. Commercial catalogues carry richer human metadata than free fonts do, so their results cannot be reproduced from our labels. Young GitHub projects may disappear. I did not run Monotype's search, so I cannot say how it answers 'fast movement or action'.
evaluation_hook: Copy two things: fontmap's held-out Google-tag recovery (precision@k against chance) for the label side, and Adobe's three-level rating (very good, ok, not good) on rendered result grids for the search side, with two baselines as Adobe did (random and 'very common' fonts). Use 20 to 30 requests, with 'fast movement or action' among them, and report the share rated very good or ok.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: Use partly, as a source of patterns and a test design, not of data. (1) Borrow Adobe Express's shape: request words go to intents, and each font carries 5 to 7 intent words; for us a small intents.json for the weakly tagged rows first (567 rows), written in Google's vocabulary plus a few shape words. (2) Borrow fontmap's held-out Google-tag scoring and Adobe's three-level rating for the evaluation item. (3) Treat Monotype AI Search as proof of demand and of the interface (explanations, follow-ups, which the app already has), not as a method: nothing is disclosed to copy. (4) Skip Fontjoy and IDEO (pairing and map only), and Typewolf and Fonts In Use as data (curation and a robots.txt that blocks automation); use them by hand to choose test requests and a few known 'fast' typefaces as ground truth. (5) TypeSeek confirms the same stack idea (a model describes each font image once, plus embeddings), but it was created on 2026-09-17 (about two weeks old today), has no licence and no published numbers. Where it sits: it ranks the other items rather than competing with them; it says per-font signal for the 339 non-Google rows and a proper test matter more than another vocabulary. Smallest first step: write the 25-request list and the rating sheet with the three-level scale, run today's Haiku search as the baseline on the 'fast movement or action' request and a few others, and keep those grids to compare with the first improvement.
